Teaching abroad is the most accessible paid work overseas available to a native English speaker, and for many people it is the first time a passport becomes an income rather than an expense. This article covers how the visa side actually works, because the teaching certificate is the easy part.

''General information, not legal advice. Every country sets its own rules and changes them; verify with the destination's consulate or immigration authority.''

== They pay to bring you, and they house you ==

The fact that gets buried in every discussion of this work: a standard full-time contract abroad routinely includes '''airfare''' and '''housing''', arranged before you arrive.

Stated plainly, that means a person with a passport, a degree in any subject and a teaching certificate can be '''offered a job, a flight and somewhere to live''' — in that order, from a standing start, without savings and without a deposit. For someone who needs to move out of a family home, leave a bad situation, or restart somewhere else entirely, this is one of the only legitimate routes that does not require capital first.

It is worth being exact about what "housing provided" usually means, because expectations cause most of the disappointment: typically a small furnished flat or a room, sometimes shared, near the school, with utilities either included or deducted. It is accommodation, not luxury. It is also the single largest cost of living in any country, removed.

The same structure covers the return: airfare is commonly '''reimbursed on completion of the contract''', which is both a benefit and a retention mechanism — leave early and you usually forfeit it.

== The recurring pattern ==

Across most destinations the shape is the same:

# '''An employer sponsors you.''' You do not generally apply for a work visa on your own initiative; a school, language institute or government programme files on your behalf once it has offered you a position. Finding the job precedes the visa, not the other way round.
# '''A bachelor's degree is frequently required''' — in any subject. This is usually an '''immigration''' requirement rather than the employer's preference, which is why it is rarely negotiable even when the employer wants you.
# '''A teaching certificate.''' 120 hours is the market's informal floor. See [[Teaching English Abroad TEFL and TESOL]].
# '''A criminal record check''', often required to be '''apostilled''' — authenticated for international use under the Hague Apostille Convention. This step surprises people and takes weeks; start it early.
# '''Authenticated degree certificates''', frequently also apostilled.
# '''A medical check''', sometimes on arrival.

The apostille requirement is the single most common cause of a delayed start. The document must usually be authenticated in the country that issued it, which is difficult to arrange once you have already left.

== Government placement programmes ==

Several countries recruit foreign teachers directly rather than leaving it to private schools. These are generally the safest entry route — the employer is a ministry or a public programme, the visa handling is routine, and the terms are published:

* '''JET Programme''' (Japan) — places assistant language teachers and coordinators in public schools and government offices.
* '''EPIK''' (South Korea) — the public-school English programme.
* '''Auxiliares de conversación''' (Spain) — language assistants in Spanish schools.
* '''Fulbright English Teaching Assistantships''' — placements in a wide range of countries, administered through the Fulbright programme.

Application cycles for these run far ahead of the start date, often by six months or more.

== What the package usually contains ==

A typical full-time contract abroad includes some combination of salary, provided or subsidised '''housing''', '''airfare''' reimbursed on completion of contract, paid holidays, health insurance and visa sponsorship. The housing and airfare elements are why a modest nominal salary frequently nets out better than it looks against a domestic job.

== Teaching online ==

Online teaching requires no visa, which is its principal advantage and its principal limitation. You can start immediately, from anywhere, and build hours and references — but you are being paid by a platform at platform rates, usually without benefits, and you are not establishing residence or a local employment record anywhere.

The strategic use of online teaching is as the '''bridge''': it funds the certificate, accumulates documented hours and references, and makes the in-person application credible. See the online-and-in-person comparison in [[Teaching English Abroad TEFL and TESOL]].

== It is not only language ==

The English-teaching market is the biggest door but not the only one. The same pattern — employer sponsorship, credential, authenticated documents — governs international schools hiring subject teachers, universities hiring instructors and researchers, and religious organisations bringing in ministers and practitioners. For the American outbound case the destination's rules govern; for the inbound case, see [[The R-1 Religious Worker Visa]], [[The O-1 Visa Extraordinary Ability]] and [[Teaching and Exchange Visas J-1 and Coming to Teach in America]].

A person with a subject qualification, a teaching certificate and a clean record is employable in far more places than they usually imagine. See [[Stacking Credentials and the Bilateral Career Path]].

Programmes are listed at [https://credentials.soapbox.community/industry/teaching-english credentials.soapbox.community].
